results.abstractText: Lethal congenital contracture syndrome 3 (LCCS3, MIM #611369) is a rare autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function (LOF) variants in PIP5K1C, reported in only two families to date. It typically presents with severe fetal akinesia, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, and perinatal lethality due to respiratory insufficiency case. Herein, we report a new case with survival beyond birth. Prenatal findings included clubfeet with preserved amniotic fluid volume and fetal movements. The infant was delivered by cesarean section at 37 + 7 weeks following breech presentation and developed respiratory distress requiring 14 days of ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed bilateral talipes equinovarus, flexion contractures of the knees, restricted hip mobility, clenched hands with flexion contractures of the third and fourth fingers, and hyperextension of the second and fifth fingers. Neurologically, he had encephalopathy, profound hypotonia with a frog posture, and abnormal neonatal reflexes with a discontinuous background pattern on cerebral function monitoring. Additional observed features were bilateral optic atrophy and hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia responsive to Diazoxide. Trio genome sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic splice-site variant in PIP5K1C (c.1127+1G>A, NM_012398.3). The infant died at 6 months from multisystemic failure. Further studies are warranted to elucidate the pathomechanisms underlying the PIP5K1C defect and its phenotypic consequences.

results.abstractText: Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) supports precision medicine in cancer care, but accurate assessment of missense variant pathogenicity, especially for variants without established consensus, remains challenging. Various computational tools have been developed for variant functional prediction, but most current tools rely solely on variant-level features and do not capture the clinical context of individual patients. To address this limitation, we developed MARiO (Missense Alteration Risk identifier in Oncology), a machine-learning model that integrates variant-level features and patient-level clinical and genomic contexts to effectively predict the pathogenicity of missense variants in cancer. We collected a total of 10,180 missense variants from 1271 patients and evaluated candidate features for their association with variant pathogenicity, identifying informative features including in silico functional predictions, population allele frequency, variant allele frequency, and tumor mutational burden. Using these selected features, MARiO was developed with extreme gradient boosting. The model integrates multiple in silico prediction tools and patient-specific genomic contexts while accommodating missing values frequently observed in real-world data. MARiO outperformed existing tools, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922. The model demonstrated strong generalizability across multiple external datasets and showed consistency with real-world molecular treatment proposals. MARiO offers a robust and clinically relevant approach for missense variant pathogenicity assessment by integrating variant- and patient-level features and serves as a valuable tool to support clinical decision-making.

results.abstractText: Defects in motile cilia cause a range of disorders, including heterotaxy (HTX), congenital heart disease (CHD), and primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Although these conditions often co-occur, the genetic and mechanistic bases for tissue-specific manifestations remain poorly understood. Here, we identify compound heterozygous variants in DAW1, a dynein arm assembly factor, in a proband with an HTX/laterality defect spectrum, presenting with complex CHD without extracardiac organ malposition and no evidence of PCD. Whole-genome sequencing revealed a maternally inherited canonical splice-site variant (c.648+1 G > A, chr2:227,903,110 G > A (GRCh38)) and a paternally inherited missense variant (c.341 G > A; p.Arg114Gln, chr2: 227,893,818 G > A (GRCh38)), both classified as variants of uncertain significance under ACMG/AMP guidelines. Using Xenopus tropicalis, we show that Daw1 depletion disrupts left-right patterning, cardiac looping, and mucociliary flow, all of which are rescued by wild-type human DAW1. Functional testing of patient alleles showed notable tissue specificity: p.Arg114Gln rescued mucociliary flow but did not restore left-right patterning, while the splice-site variant resulted in a complete loss of function in both contexts. These findings closely match the proband's clinical phenotype and provide strong functional evidence to support reclassifying c.648+1 G > A as likely pathogenic and p.Arg114Gln as a context-dependent hypomorphic allele. This study establishes functional criteria for interpreting DAW1 variants, shows how developmental context clarifies genotype-phenotype relationships, and highlights how in vivo models can support ACMG reclassification of unresolved HTX-related variants.

results.abstractText: STXBP1 variants are a frequent cause of early onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies and related neurodevelopmental disorders, but the clinical interpretation of these variants remains a major challenge. Most reported STXBP1 missense variants are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), complicating diagnosis, counseling, and patient eligibility for precision therapies. Here, we developed EpiPred, a gene-specific machine learning classifier that predicts the pathogenicity of STXBP1 missense variants and tests these predictions using empirical evidence from well-established cellular assays. Trained on a curated set of pathogenic and benign variants, EpiPred outperformed global prediction tools in accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. We validated the model's predictions using variant effect assays that measure protein abundance, solubility, stability, and interaction with the SNARE complex partner syntaxin 1. These biochemical readouts aligned closely with model outputs and enabled reclassification of several possibly misdiagnosed variants, which warrant further validation and clinical reevaluation. We deployed EpiPred in an interactive web application that allows clinicians, researchers, and patients to explore predictions for all possible STXBP1 missense variants. By identifying likely pathogenic STXBP1 variants, including those that may respond to emerging therapies, such as protein stabilizers. By coupling gene-calibrated machine learning with orthogonal variant-effect assays and public deployment, EpiPred provides a transferable framework for VUS resolution, trial enrichment, and precision diagnosis across clinically actionable Mendelian disease genes.

results.abstractText: PROKR2 is an established gene associated with Kallmann syndrome (KS), and preclinical studies have suggested a possible role in tumor development. In this study, we report a patient with KS and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) colon cancer and aim to explore the potential association between PROKR2 variants and MSI-H status in colorectal cancer (CRC). Peripheral blood samples from the proband and his parents underwent whole-exome sequencing (WES) to identify germline variants. The WES revealed that both the proband and his father carried a likely pathogenic variant in the KS-associated gene PROKR2 (NM_144773.4:c.337T>C, p.Tyr113His). To place this case in a broader context, we performed exploratory bioinformatic analyses of somatic PROKR2 variants in two public CRC cohorts, DFCI-CRC and TCGA-CRC, although these cohort analyses cannot inform germline risk. In the DFCI-CRC cohort, PROKR2 somatic variant status showed no statistically significant association with MSI-H status in either the unadjusted or TMB-adjusted analysis. In the TCGA-CRC cohort, PROKR2 somatic variants were associated with higher unadjusted odds of MSI-H (OR = 5.50, 95% CI = 1.003-30.20, p = 0.0248, BH-adjusted q = 0.0495). After TMB adjustment, this positive association was not retained and the adjusted estimate was in the opposite direction (adjusted OR = 0.093, 95% CI = 0.014-0.549, p = 0.00875, BH-adjusted q = 0.0175). Accordingly, this case report describes the co-occurrence of PROKR2-related KS and MSI-H CRC in a single patient, although a causal relationship between PROKR2-related KS and CRC remains unestablished.

results.abstractText:
Background

Many commonly used computational tools for variant effect prediction exhibit ancestry-related bias because they are trained on clinical or population datasets that under-represent global diversity, leading to uneven and sometimes unfair variant classification across ancestries. Multiplexed assays of variant effect (MAVEs) and population-free variant effect predictors (VEPs) instead offer alternatives that are unbiased with respect to human ancestry, providing classification evidence that generalises across populations.

Methods

Here, we evaluate MAVE- and VEP-based classification across five cancer-associated genes with high-quality MAVE datasets, focusing primarily on three leading population-free VEPs: GEMME, EVE, and CPT-1.

Results

We find that MAVEs are more conservative and decisive in classification, assigning fewer variants to the pathogenic category while yielding fewer indeterminate classifications when calibrated to ACMG/AMP guidelines. Although MAVEs show heightened sensitivity in functionally assayed regions, VEPs identify a broader range of pathogenic variants overall. By combining clinical evidence strengths from MAVEs and VEPs, we reclassify over 90% of variants of uncertain significance across the SG10K_Health and Mexico City Prospective Study reference datasets as at least likely benign or likely pathogenic. We further isolate variants where MAVE- and VEP-based classifications are discordant, highlighting method-specific limitations.

Conclusions

Together, these findings clarify the complementary strengths of experimental and computational classification approaches and provide a path to less biased and more equitable variant interpretation in clinical genomics, helping to mitigate disparities in diagnosis across ancestries.

results.abstractText: The tumor suppressor RAD51D is essential for homologous recombination (HR). Pathogenic variants in RAD51D are associated with breast and ovarian cancers. However, most clinical missense variants are of uncertain significance. Here, we report a multiplex assay of variant effect to test 6,888 RAD51D coding variants for loss-of-function. The resulting variant-to-function map perfectly separates known pathogenic and benign variants and is validated by orthogonal HR and biochemical assays across 70 clinical variants. Our screen shows that variants in the DNA-binding or ATPase core most severely compromise HR, and we identify the RAD51D-RAD51C interface within the BCDX2 complex as essential for regulating its ATPase activity. We hypothesize that, paradoxically, the primary function of RAD51D is to slow the ATPase activity of BCDX2, thereby allowing sufficient time and space for RAD51 filament assembly. Together, we identify hotspots of deleterious RAD51D variants and uncover the mechanisms by which variants compromise its biochemical functions.

results.abstractText:
Introduction

Bleomycin is a key component of curative-intent chemotherapy for germ cell tumours (GCT) and Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL), but its use is limited by bleomycin-induced pneumonitis (BIP). Although established clinical risk factors predict some cases, BIP also occurs without these. Preclinical models and small human studies implicate a contribution of drug metabolism, oxidative stress, immune and fibrotic pathways that may contribute to susceptibility. We aimed to identify germline genetic contributors to BIP in predominantly clinically low-risk patients to improve risk stratification in GCT and HL.

Methods

We retrospectively identified 21 patients (13 GCT, 8 HL) who developed clinically significant BIP despite predominantly low clinical risk. Clinical data were collected and, where possible, blood samples were obtained for whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Analysis focused on a curated BIP-risk gene panel, derived from a literature review of genes/alleles implicated in BIP, alongside polygenic risk scores (PRS) for relevant lung and autoinflammatory/autoimmune pathology.

Results

Median age was 39 (GCT) and 49 (HL) years; 67% were life-time non-smokers. Most patients with BIP experienced CTCAE grade < 3 (76%), and 52% received corticosteroids. WGS was performed in 18 individuals. Missense variants with low general population allele frequency were observed in 9 genes within the curated panel, although the significance of these remains unknown. PRS analysis in 12 individuals of European ancestry showed no association of BIP with established PRS for lung disease or autoinflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Conclusion

Biologically plausible candidate germline variants involved in lung surfactant biology and inflammatory signaling were identified. These exploratory findings provide candidate genes and pathways for future investigations into the genetic basis of BIP.

results.abstractText: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing, fatal neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. Clinical manifestations include progressive muscle weakness, amyotrophy, fasciculations, dysphagia, and fatal respiratory failure. The median survival after symptom onset is typically 2 to 5 years. Despite its severity, the epidemiological profile and genetic landscape of ALS in Latin American populations, particularly in Mexico, remain unclear. In this study, we evaluated the mutational spectrum of the SOD1 gene in a Mexican cohort of 156 ALS patients. Using high-resolution melting (HRM) analysis and Sanger sequencing, we identified 22 SOD1 variants in 42 of 156 patients (overall variant carrier frequency, 26.92%). Pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants were found in 21 patients (13.5%). Notably, 5 of the 22 variants were novel, expanding the spectrum of SOD1 variants. The variant carrier frequency identified in this study is higher than that reported for European populations but similar to frequencies observed in Asian populations. Our results highlight the distinct genetic heterogeneity of ALS in Mexico and demonstrate that HRM is a rapid and effective method for identifying SOD1 gene variants.

results.abstractText: Background/Objectives: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by alterations in brain development and function, frequently associated with complex genetic architectures. The widespread implementation of next-generation sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing (WES), has substantially increased the identification of potentially disease-associated variants, shifting the major challenge from variant detection to their interpretation and prioritization. This review examines the emerging contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to WES variant interpretation in NDDs, with particular emphasis on AI-assisted variant prioritization and protein structural modelling. Methods: We reviewed conventional computational and emerging AI-driven approaches applicable to different stages of WES interpretation, including variant pathogenicity and functional-effect prediction, evolutionary conservation, splicing assessment, phenotype-informed prioritization, and protein structure prediction. Their methodological principles, applications, and major limitations were critically examined within the context of neurodevelopmental genomics. Results: AI and machine-learning approaches increasingly integrate genomic, phenotypic, functional, and structural information, supporting phenotype-aware candidate prioritization and molecular contextualization of selected variants. However, computational outputs are affected by model-specific limitations and should not be considered independent evidence of pathogenicity. Their added value depends primarily on the complementarity and biological relevance of the information provided, rather than on predictor concordance alone. Conclusions: This narrative review highlights that AI-assisted WES interpretation should prioritize complementary, mechanism-relevant evidence over computational concordance. AI-assisted tools should therefore be selected according to variant class and disease mechanism and integrated with independent clinical, genetic, and functional evidence.

results.abstractText: Background: Athletic performance is a result of interaction between genetic and environmental factors, including training, nutrition, rest, hormonal and psychophysiological status. Numerous genes and polymorphisms can influence key physiological processes, such as muscle contractility, energy metabolism, oxidative capacity, and cardiovascular efficiency. Among these, the ACTN3 gene, and in particular the polymorphism rs1815739 (NM_001104.4:c.1729C>T; p.Arg577Ter), is well known for its association with athletic performance, but emerging evidence suggests broader effects on metabolic and inflammatory phenotypes. Methods: For this study, 109 elite athletes were enrolled and genotyped for ACTN3 c.1729C>T by Sanger sequencing. Moreover, biochemical markers, such as creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP), lipid profile, adiponectin, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), were examined. Finally, to better investigate the association between genotype and athletic performance, the genotypes and the results of standardized physical tests were correlated in a small exploratory subgroup of 28 professional basketball athletes. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; non-normally distributed variables were summarized as median [IQR] and analyzed with non-parametric methods. Genotype comparisons were adjusted for multiple testing using the Holm procedure, and principal biochemical models were adjusted for age, BMI, sex, and ancestry. Results: The c.1729C>T genotype distribution differed between the two ancestry groups (exact p = 0.049), and all three variants were compatible with Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium within the ancestry groups. No biochemical genotype association remained statistically significant after Holm correction. In the performance subgroup, no genotype-performance association remained significant after Holm correction. Conclusions: In this cohort, the corrected analyses did not provide robust evidence for genotype-dependent biochemical or performance effects. The results are exploratory and require replication in larger cohorts, considering ancestry and gender differences.

journal.title: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis

results.abstractText:
Background

Hemostasis is a tightly regulated system in which disruption of coagulation genes can cause bleeding or thrombotic disorders. Despite extensive variant discovery, it remains unclear whether coagulation genes share uniform or gene-specific patterns of evolutionary constraint and population variation.

Objectives

To characterize evolutionary constraint and population variation across coagulation genes using large-scale genomic data.

Methods

We performed a population-genomic analysis of 34 genes associated with inherited bleeding, fibrinolytic, and thrombotic disorders using Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD) v4.1.1 data from more than 800,000 individuals. We evaluated gene-level constraint metrics, including loss-of-function observed/expected ratios, loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound fraction, missense constraint scores, and synonymous variation metrics. We quantified rare and very rare variant burden after normalization for coding sequence length, assessed predicted functional impact using CADD and REVEL scores, evaluated nucleotide-level evolutionary conservation using phylogenetic P value scores, and characterized ClinVar pathogenic, uncertain, and benign variants identified in gnomAD.

Results

Hemostatic genes demonstrated a continuous spectrum of evolutionary constraint rather than uniform intolerance to genetic variation. Genes including F8, F9, F2, VWF, MYH9, SERPINC1, and PROS1 showed strong depletion of damaging variation, whereas GP6, GP1BB, F12, VKORC1, MCFD2, and LMAN1 showed greater tolerance. Rare variant density differed substantially across genes even after adjustment for coding sequence length. ClinVar pathogenic variants identified in gnomAD were enriched at evolutionarily conserved sites and displayed marked gene-specific differences in variant class distribution, particularly among missense variants.

Conclusions

The hemostatic system is shaped by heterogeneous evolutionary pressures, resulting in gene-specific patterns of constraint and variation tolerance. Integrating population genomics, evolutionary conservation, and clinical annotations provides a framework for understanding genetic variation across bleeding, thrombotic, and fibrinolytic disorders.

results.abstractText:
Background

In males, MECP2 loss of function was long thought to be lethal or uniformly severe, and affected boys remain under-recognised. Their clinical range is still poorly defined.

Methods

We assembled a multicentre Turkish series of 22 hemizygous male probands ascertained through routine diagnostic testing rather than severe-phenotype registries. Variants were classified under the ClinGen Expert Panel specification for MECP2 (GN036, version 6.0.0) and its combining rules, with the Panel's ClinVar classifications adopted where available. Phenotypic analysis was restricted to the 21 probands with pathogenic, likely pathogenic or uncertain variants.

Results

The 22 probands carried 17 distinct variants (11 missense, 5 frameshift and one 3' untranslated region deletion), of which 2 were classified as pathogenic, 1 likely pathogenic, 13 uncertain and 1 benign (3, 4, 14 and 1 probands, respectively). Where recorded, intellectual disability or developmental delay affected 7 of 7 probands with pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and 8 of 10 with uncertain variants; seizures affected 2 of 3 and 8 of 10, respectively. Growth or head-circumference findings, recorded in 9 of 21 probands, included obesity or overgrowth (5), microcephaly (4, one borderline) and short stature (3). A maternal carrier was identified in 6 of 22 families (five laboratory-confirmed); the other 16 mothers were untested, so no de novo event was confirmed. Second-locus findings, reported by referring laboratories in 3 probands, could not be independently reclassified.

Conclusions

In this diagnostically ascertained series, phenotypes observed among males carrying MECP2 variants were graded rather than uniformly severe. Fourteen of the 21 probands carry variants of uncertain significance, in whom causation is not established, so the range that may be attributed to MECP2 rests on seven individuals carrying variants classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic under the stated criteria. In one of them, published functional data on the identical variant conflict with its pathogenic classification, so attribution of his phenotype to MECP2 remains uncertain. These provisional observations support a low threshold for MECP2 testing in males with unexplained neurodevelopmental presentations, attention to growth as well as head circumference, and consideration of additional loci.

results.abstractText: Population-scale sequencing can quantify genotypes associated with von Willebrand disease (VWD), but these frequencies cannot be translated directly into clinically manifest disease without phenotype and penetrance data. We therefore estimated subtype-specific VWD-associated genotype frequencies in RGC-ME, compared them with gnomAD, and examined which analytical assumptions limit clinical interpretation. Germline VWF variants classified in ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) on 1 August 2026 were normalized to GRCh38 and matched exactly to both resources. Subtypes were assigned only from unambiguous ClinVar phenotypes, and expected genotype frequencies were calculated from cumulative allele frequencies under dominant or recessive models. ClinVar contained 459 unique sequence-level P/LP alleles; 116 were shared by RGC-ME and gnomAD, 20 occurred only in RGC-ME, 68 only in gnomAD, and 255 in neither extract. The expected RGC-ME genotype frequencies per million individuals were 198, 16, 43, and 224 for types 1, 2A, 2B, and 2M, respectively, and 22.88 and 0.008 for types 2N and 3. Corresponding RGC-ME/gnomAD ratios ranged from 0.753 to 0.911. Shared allele frequencies were strongly concordant (Pearson r = 0.933; Spearman ρ = 0.887), although 238/459 alleles lacked an unambiguous subtype assignment. The cumulative frequency of P/LP VWF alleles was similar across resources, whereas subtype-specific expected genotype frequencies varied with phenotype annotation, the contribution of recurrent alleles, inheritance assumptions, and incomplete variant capture. Population databases can therefore quantify allele burden and model the frequency of VWD-associated genotypes, but clinical registries are required to determine penetrance, genotype-phenotype relationships, and the prevalence of clinically diagnosed VWD.
